posts.title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
This bill expands the authority of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to provide information to certain persons (e.g., trademark or copyright owners) regarding suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
Under current law, if CBP suspects that merchandise is being imported in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws, it may request assistance from specified persons when determining whether the merchandise is imported in violation of these laws. To permit the party to conduct examination and testing, CBP must provide them with specified information that appears on the merchandise and its packaging and labels.
This bill (1) expands the definition of person to allow CBP to request assistance from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported merchandise, and (2) expands the scope of information that CBP is authorized to share with others to include information on and images of packing materials and containers.
The bill allows CBP to request this assistance if it has a reasonable suspicion (currently, suspects) that the merchandise being imported is in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws.
Additionally, CBP may provide a person with nonpublic information about the imported merchandise that was generated by an online marketplace or similar market platform, express consignment operator, freight forwarder, or any other entity that plays a role in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the merchandise into the United States and has been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. CBP must provide the person with notification of the transmitted information.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee
posts.meta: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Blake Moore (R-UT)
posts.whatsNext: Takes effect (on enactment unless the text sets other dates)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) more power to get outside help when it suspects that imported goods infringe on trademarks or copyrights. Under current law, CBP can ask certain people, such as trademark or copyright owners, to help decide whether goods are illegal copies, and it can share specified label and packaging information so they can examine and test the goods. The bill widens both parts of that system.

First, it lets CBP ask for help from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported goods, not just the specified groups covered now. Second, it expands the information CBP can share to include information about and images of packing materials and containers, not only what appears on the goods and their labels.

The bill also lowers the threshold for asking for help. Right now CBP must suspect a violation. Under the bill, it may act if it has a reasonable suspicion that the goods violate certain trademark and copyright laws.

In addition, CBP may give a person nonpublic information about the imported goods that was generated by an online marketplace or similar platform, an express consignment operator, a freight forwarder, or any other entity involved in selling, importing, or moving the goods into the United States. That information must have been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. When CBP shares it, it must notify the person that the information was sent.

posts.title: Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to increase the amounts payable for wartime disability compensation, additional compensation for dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation for surviving spouses and children. Specifically, the VA must increase the amounts by the same percentage as the cost-of-living increase in benefits for Social Security recipients that is effective on December 1, 2026. The act requires the VA to publish the amounts payable, as increased, in the Federal Register.
The VA is authorized to make a similar adjustment to the rates of disability compensation payable to persons who have not received compensation for service-connected disability or death.

aiSummaries.text:
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to raise several benefit payments for veterans and their families. The payments covered are wartime disability compensation, extra compensation for dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation for surviving spouses and children.

The increase is set by the same percentage as the cost-of-living increase for Social Security recipients that takes effect on December 1, 2026. In other words, the veterans' payments rise by that same percentage.

The VA must publish the new, higher payment amounts in the Federal Register, the official government publication where such notices appear.

The VA is also allowed, though not required, to make a similar adjustment to disability compensation rates for people who have not received compensation for a service-connected disability or death.

posts.title: To authorize the Secretary of the Army to convey to the State of North Carolina a certain parcel of real property located at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, on which the State shall construct a veterans’ State home, and for other purposes.
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
This bill authorizes the Department of the Army to transfer, without compensation or other consideration, all right, title, and interest to a specified 20-acre parcel of land on Fort Bragg to the State of North Carolina for the purpose of constructing a state home under the jurisdiction of the North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs. (A state home is a home established by a state for veterans who are disabled by age, disease, or otherwise and are incapable of earning a living because of such disability. The term also includes a home that furnishes nursing home care for veterans.)
Specifically, the bill authorizes the conveyance of a 20-acre parcel of land situated on the Fort Bragg Training Area in Harnett County, North Carolina, that is commonly referred to as Parcel 3B.
The State of North Carolina must cover all costs to carry out the conveyance.
If the Department of the Army determines the property is not being used for activities related to a state home, all right, title, and interest in the property may revert to the United States.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Armed Services Committee · Rep. Richard Hudson (R-NC)
posts.whatsNext: Takes effect (on enactment unless the text sets other dates)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill lets the Army give a 20-acre piece of land on Fort Bragg, known as Parcel 3B, to the State of North Carolina for free. The land is in Harnett County, on the Fort Bragg Training Area. The state plans to use it to build a state home for veterans, and the home would be run by the North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs.

A state home is a home set up by a state for veterans who are disabled by age, illness, or some other cause and cannot earn a living because of that disability. The term also covers a home that provides nursing home care for veterans.

North Carolina has to pay all the costs of carrying out the transfer.

If the Army decides the land is not being used for activities related to the state home, the land can go back to the United States.

posts.title: Chip EQUIP Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Commerce, Science, and Transportation, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute and an amendment to the title, without written report
posts.summary:
Chip Equipment Quality, Usefulness, and Integrity Protection Act of 2025 or the Chip EQUIP Act
This bill prohibits companies that receive certain federal funds from purchasing specified semiconductor manufacturing equipment made by foreign entities of concern (e.g., companies owned or controlled by China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia) or their subsidiaries for the federally funded project.
The CHIPS Act of 2022, which became law in August 2022, appropriated funding for the Department of Commerce to carry out the CHIPS for America provisions enacted in the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021. These provisions included appropriations for financial incentives to expand domestic manufacturing capacities across the semiconductor supply chain, as well as for research and development programs.
Under the bill, Commerce must include in the terms of each agreement with a covered entity (e.g., companies receiving CHIPS funds) prohibitions with respect to a project relating to the procurement, installation, or use of the specified semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The prohibitions must be effective for 10 years beginning on the date on which the agreement is signed.
The bill authorizes Commerce to waive these prohibitions under certain circumstances, such as if the specified semiconductor manufacturing equipment is not produced in the United States or an allied or partner country in sufficient and reasonably available quantities or of a satisfactory quality to support established or expected production capabilities.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would stop companies that receive certain federal funds from buying specified chip-making equipment made by foreign companies of concern, or by their subsidiaries, for the federally funded project. Those foreign companies include firms owned or controlled by China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia.

The background is the CHIPS Act of 2022, which Congress passed in August 2022. That law provided money for the Department of Commerce to carry out the CHIPS for America provisions, which were first enacted in the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021. The money was meant to help expand domestic chip manufacturing across the semiconductor supply chain and to fund research and development.

Under the bill, the Department of Commerce must write these restrictions into each agreement with a company receiving CHIPS funds. The restrictions cover buying, installing, or using the specified equipment for the project. They would last 10 years from the date the agreement is signed.

The bill also lets Commerce waive these restrictions in certain situations. One example is when the specified equipment is not made in the United States or in an allied or partner country in sufficient amounts, at reasonably available supply, or at a satisfactory quality to support current or expected production.

posts.title: COLLUDE Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Commerce, Science, and Transportation, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Curtailing Online Limitations that Lead Unconstitutionally to Democracy's Erosion Act or the COLLUDE Act
This bill limits federal liability protection, sometimes referred to as Section 230 protection, that generally precludes providers and users of an interactive computer service (e.g., a social media company) from being held legally responsible for content provided by a third party.
Specifically, the bill removes the protection if a provider restricts access to or availability of content containing political speech because of a governmental request unless the request serves a legitimate law enforcement or national security purpose.
In addition, the bill changes legal procedures for applying the protection. Currently, the protection serves as broad immunity that typically allows the early dismissal of lawsuits, thereby preempting lawsuits and statutes that impose liability for third-party content. This bill makes the protection an affirmative defense, which means the provider or user must prove that the protection applies before the lawsuit may be dismissed.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-MO)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would weaken a legal shield that currently protects online services, such as social media companies, and their users from being held responsible for content posted by others. The shield is often called Section 230.

Under the bill, that protection would be removed in one situation: when a provider limits access to content containing political speech because the government asked it to. The exception is if the government request serves a legitimate law enforcement or national security purpose.

The bill also changes how the protection works in court. Right now it acts as broad immunity, which usually lets a judge throw out a lawsuit early. Under the bill, it would instead be an affirmative defense, meaning the provider or user would have to prove the protection applies before the lawsuit could be dismissed.

posts.title: Common Cents Act
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
Common Cents Act
This bill ends the production of the penny for general circulation, requires rounding to an amount divisible by five for the payment or transfer of cash, and allows the nickel to be composed of different material.
The Department of the Treasury must stop producing the penny, except to meet collector needs. The penny shall continue to be legal tender.
Any person selling goods or services in a cash transaction, entering into other transfers of cash, or paying cash wages to an employee must round the payment up or down in accordance with the bill.
The bill also allows Treasury to discontinue the minting for circulation of any coin if Treasury follows procedures as outlined by the bill, including providing notice and a briefing to Congress.
The Federal Reserve Board must periodically report on a strategic plan for the acceptance of penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that provide services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.
Finally, the bill allows for a different material composition of the nickel. In addition to being made from an alloy of copper and nickel, the nickel may also be clad with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.

Under the bill, anyone who sells goods or services for cash, makes other cash transfers, or pays employees in cash would have to round the amount up or down so it can be divided evenly by five. This rounding rule would apply to those cash payments and transfers.

The bill also lets the Treasury stop making any coin for circulation, but only if it follows the steps set out in the bill. Those steps include giving notice to Congress and providing it a briefing.

The Federal Reserve Board would have to report regularly on a strategic plan for accepting penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that offer services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.

Finally, the bill would allow the nickel to be made from a different material. Besides the current copper and nickel alloy, a nickel could be made with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.

This bill requires federal agencies to publish a searchable, online database of information about certain settlement agreements entered into by the agency. The database must include

whether the agreement resolves a civil or criminal claim (or both),

To extent practicable, the bill also applies retroactively to covered settlement agreements that were entered into on or after January 1, 2015, and remain in effect on or after the date of enactment.
The OMB must issue guidance to implement the bill.

posts.title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
This bill expands the authority of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to provide information to certain persons (e.g., trademark or copyright owners) regarding suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
Under current law, if CBP suspects that merchandise is being imported in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws, it may request assistance from specified persons when determining whether the merchandise is imported in violation of these laws. To permit the party to conduct examination and testing, CBP must provide them with specified information that appears on the merchandise and its packaging and labels.
This bill (1) expands the definition of person to allow CBP to request assistance from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported merchandise, and (2) expands the scope of information that CBP is authorized to share with others to include information on and images of packing materials and containers.
The bill allows CBP to request this assistance if it has a reasonable suspicion (currently, suspects) that the merchandise being imported is in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws.
Additionally, CBP may provide a person with nonpublic information about the imported merchandise that was generated by an online marketplace or similar market platform, express consignment operator, freight forwarder, or any other entity that plays a role in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the merchandise into the United States and has been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. CBP must provide the person with notification of the transmitted information.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee
posts.meta: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Blake Moore (R-UT)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) more power to get outside help when it suspects that imported goods infringe on trademarks or copyrights. Under current law, CBP can ask certain people, such as trademark or copyright owners, to help decide whether goods are illegal copies, and it can share specified label and packaging information so they can examine and test the goods. The bill widens both parts of that system.

First, it lets CBP ask for help from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported goods, not just the specified groups covered now. Second, it expands the information CBP can share to include information about and images of packing materials and containers, not only what appears on the goods and their labels.

The bill also lowers the threshold for asking for help. Right now CBP must suspect a violation. Under the bill, it may act if it has a reasonable suspicion that the goods violate certain trademark and copyright laws.

In addition, CBP may give a person nonpublic information about the imported goods that was generated by an online marketplace or similar platform, an express consignment operator, a freight forwarder, or any other entity involved in selling, importing, or moving the goods into the United States. That information must have been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. When CBP shares it, it must notify the person that the information was sent.

After the transfer, Arkansas would have to name the land the Crossett Experimental State Forest. The state must also work with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, including giving the universities reasonable access to the forest for research and teaching.

The transfer would be subject to any valid rights that already exist on the land. Arkansas would receive the land at no cost, and the transfer would be made by quitclaim deed, which passes whatever interest the government holds without a guarantee of clear title. Arkansas would also pay all the costs of the transfer, including surveys and other administrative expenses.

posts.title: GRID Power Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Natural Resources, without amendment, without written report
posts.summary:
Guaranteeing Reliability through the Interconnection of Dispatchable Power Act or the GRID Power Act
This bill requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to issue and periodically review a rule that revises the approval process for interconnection requests of generating units that produce electricity to prioritize dispatchable power projects (e.g., certain fossil fuel projects).
Under the bill, dispatchable power generally refers to an electric energy generation resource, such as a generating unit that produces electricity from fossil fuels, capable of providing known and forecastable electric supply in time intervals necessary to ensure grid reliability. Currently, FERC receives interconnection requests from those projects and other generating units, such as units that produce electricity from renewable energy. Interconnection requests are requests from generating units to connect to the high voltage transmission lines of the electric grid.
First, the rule must address the efficiency and effectiveness of the existing procedures for processing interconnection requests to ensure that new dispatchable power projects that improve grid reliability and resource adequacy can interconnect to the electric grid quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably.
Second, the rule must revise the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Procedures, and the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Agreement as appropriate, to authorize transmission providers to submit proposals to FERC to prioritize new dispatchable power projects that will improve grid reliability and resource adequacy by assigning those projects higher positions in the interconnection queue of the provider. FERC must review and approve or deny such proposals within 60 days after the proposal is submitted.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Energy and Natural Resources Committee · Sen. John Hoeven (R-ND)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The GRID Power Act would require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to create and regularly review a rule that changes how it handles requests to connect power plants to the high-voltage transmission lines of the electric grid. The goal is to give priority to "dispatchable" power projects, meaning plants that can supply a known and predictable amount of electricity whenever it is needed to keep the grid reliable. The bill gives fossil fuel projects as an example of this kind of power.

Right now, FERC receives connection requests from many kinds of generating units, including renewable energy projects as well as dispatchable ones. Under the bill, the rule would first have to look at whether the current procedures for handling these requests work well and efficiently. The aim is to make sure new dispatchable projects that improve grid reliability and resource adequacy can connect quickly, at reasonable cost, and reliably.

The rule would also have to update the standard procedures and agreements used for large generator connections. These updates would allow transmission providers to propose that FERC move new dispatchable projects that would improve grid reliability and resource adequacy higher in their interconnection queue, which is the line of projects waiting to connect. FERC would have to approve or deny each such proposal within 60 days of its submission.

posts.title: Critical Minerals Security Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Natural Resources, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Critical Minerals Security Act of 2025
This bill establishes requirements for the Department of the Interior related to securing U.S. access to critical minerals and rare earth element (REE) resources. Critical minerals mean any mineral, element, substance, or material designated as critical by the U.S. Geological Survey. REEs mean cerium, dysprosium, erbium, europium, gadolinium, holmium, lanthanum, lutetium, neodymium, praseodymium, promethium, samarium, scandium, terbium, thulium, ytterbium, and yttrium.
First, Interior must report on the critical mineral and REE resources, including recyclable or recycled materials containing those resources, around the world. Among other information, the report must include an assessment of the global ownership and supply of critical mineral and REE resources. Interior must submit the report within a year and every two years thereafter.
Next, Interior must establish a process to assist a U.S. person—a U.S. citizen, a non-U.S. National (alien under federal law) lawfully admitted for permanent residence, or an entity organized under U.S. laws—seeking to divest stock in mining, processing, or recycling operations for critical minerals and REEs in a foreign country with finding a purchaser that is not under the control of North Korea, China, Russia, or Iran.
Finally, Interior must develop (1) a strategy to collaborate with U.S. allies and partners to develop advanced mining, refining, separation, processing, and recycling technologies; and (2) a method for sharing related intellectual property with U.S. allies and partners to enable those countries to license those technologies and develop their resources.

posts.meta: Energy and Natural Resources Committee · Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX)

aiSummaries.text:
The Critical Minerals Security Act of 2025 requires the Department of the Interior to take steps to help secure U.S. access to critical minerals and rare earth elements (REEs). Critical minerals are any minerals, elements, substances, or materials that the U.S. Geological Survey has designated as critical. The bill lists seventeen specific rare earth elements, including cerium, dysprosium, neodymium, and yttrium.

First, Interior must report on critical mineral and REE resources around the world, including recyclable or recycled materials that contain them. The report must include, among other things, an assessment of who owns and supplies these resources globally. Interior must submit the first report within a year and then every two years after that.

Next, Interior must set up a process to help U.S. persons, meaning U.S. citizens, lawfully admitted permanent residents who are non-U.S. nationals, and entities organized under U.S. laws, who want to sell their stock in mining, processing, or recycling operations for critical minerals and REEs in a foreign country. The process is meant to help them find a buyer that is not controlled by North Korea, China, Russia, or Iran.

Finally, Interior must develop two things. The first is a strategy for working with U.S. allies and partners to develop advanced technologies for mining, refining, separating, processing, and recycling these materials. The second is a method for sharing related intellectual property with those allies and partners, so they can license the technologies and develop their own resources.

posts.title: Historic Roadways Protection Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Natural Resources, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Historic Roadways Protection Act
This bill prohibits the Bureau for Land Management (BLM) from closing historical roads on public lands in certain areas of Utah until the Federal District Court for Utah makes a decision on each of the R.S. 2477 cases, which are cases brought by Utah and counties to keep historical roads on BLM land in Utah open for public use.
By way of background, a provision of the Mining Law of 1866, commonly known as R.S. 2477, granted rights-of-way to states and counties across public lands for the construction of roads for public use in order to promote settlement of the American West. In 1976, Congress repealed R.S. 2477 when it enacted the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA), but FLPMA preserved rights-of-way that had been established under R.S. 2477. After the BLM released travel management plans that closed some historical roads, Utah and 22 counties filed lawsuits about their rights-of-way across public lands for historical roads.
Until the BLM certifies that those cases have been decided, the bill prohibits the BLM from obligating or expending federal funds to (1) finalize or implement a new travel management plan for certain travel management areas in Utah; or (2) implement, with respect to land within the boundary of Utah, the Indian Creek (Canyon Rims) Travel Management Plan, the San Rafael Desert Travel Management Plan, the San Rafael Swell Travel Management Plan, or the Labyrinth/Gemini Bridges Travel Management Plan.

R.S. 2477 was a provision of the Mining Law of 1866 that gave states and counties rights-of-way across public lands to build roads for public use, helping settle the American West. Congress repealed that provision in 1976 when it passed the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA), but FLPMA kept the rights-of-way that had already been established under R.S. 2477.

After the BLM issued travel management plans that closed some historic roads, Utah and 22 counties filed lawsuits over their rights-of-way across public lands for those roads.

Until the BLM certifies that these cases have been decided, the bill bars the agency from using federal funds to finalize or carry out a new travel management plan for certain travel management areas in Utah. posts.title: Wildfire Prevention Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Natural Resources, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
This bill establishes forest management requirements for federal lands, particularly with respect to reducing wildfires.
For example, the bill establishes annual goals to increase (1) the number of acres of Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land that are mechanically thinned (i.e., a management process related to the removal of trees and vegetation); and (2) the number of acres of Forest Service and BLM land treated by prescribed fire. By FY2029, the goals must be to increase the number of acres of each by at least 40% compared to the average number of acres of each in FY2019-FY2023.
The bill also directs the Forest Service and the BLM to (1) implement standardized procedures for tracking data relating to hazardous fuels reduction activities they carry out, and (2) develop a strategy to identify opportunities to use livestock grazing as a wildfire risk reduction tool on federal land. Additionally, the Forest Service and the Department of the Interior must establish a deployment and test bed pilot program for wildfire prevention, detection, communication, and mitigation technologies.
The bill mandates use of existing authorities for expedited environmental review for certain forest land at high risk from wildfire, insects, or disease.
Finally, the bill provides local governments and Indian tribes the right to intervene in lawsuits concerning certain projects on federal land that (1) reduce risks posed by wildfire, insects, or disease; or (2) generate revenue from harvesting timber.

posts.meta: Energy and Natural Resources Committee · Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY)

By fiscal year 2029, each of these must grow by at least 40 percent compared to the average acreage from fiscal years 2019 through 2023.

posts.title: Common Cents Act
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
Common Cents Act
This bill ends the production of the penny for general circulation, requires rounding to an amount divisible by five for the payment or transfer of cash, and allows the nickel to be composed of different material.
The Department of the Treasury must stop producing the penny, except to meet collector needs. The penny shall continue to be legal tender.
Any person selling goods or services in a cash transaction, entering into other transfers of cash, or paying cash wages to an employee must round the payment up or down in accordance with the bill.
The bill also allows Treasury to discontinue the minting for circulation of any coin if Treasury follows procedures as outlined by the bill, including providing notice and a briefing to Congress.
The Federal Reserve Board must periodically report on a strategic plan for the acceptance of penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that provide services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.
Finally, the bill allows for a different material composition of the nickel. In addition to being made from an alloy of copper and nickel, the nickel may also be clad with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, Financial Services Committee
posts.meta: Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, Financial Services Committee · Rep. Lisa McClain (R-MI)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text:
The Common Cents Act would stop the U.S. Treasury from making new pennies for everyday circulation, though the Treasury could still make them to meet the needs of coin collectors. Pennies would remain legal money.

Under the bill, anyone who sells goods or services for cash, makes other cash transfers, or pays employees in cash would have to round the amount up or down so it can be divided evenly by five. This rounding rule would apply to those cash payments and transfers.

The bill also lets the Treasury stop making any coin for circulation, but only if it follows the steps set out in the bill. Those steps include giving notice to Congress and providing it a briefing.

The Federal Reserve Board would have to report regularly on a strategic plan for accepting penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that offer services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.

Finally, the bill would allow the nickel to be made from a different material. Besides the current copper and nickel alloy, a nickel could be made with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.

posts.title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
This bill expands the authority of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to provide information to certain persons (e.g., trademark or copyright owners) regarding suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
Under current law, if CBP suspects that merchandise is being imported in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws, it may request assistance from specified persons when determining whether the merchandise is imported in violation of these laws. To permit the party to conduct examination and testing, CBP must provide them with specified information that appears on the merchandise and its packaging and labels.
This bill (1) expands the definition of person to allow CBP to request assistance from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported merchandise, and (2) expands the scope of information that CBP is authorized to share with others to include information on and images of packing materials and containers.
The bill allows CBP to request this assistance if it has a reasonable suspicion (currently, suspects) that the merchandise being imported is in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws.
Additionally, CBP may provide a person with nonpublic information about the imported merchandise that was generated by an online marketplace or similar market platform, express consignment operator, freight forwarder, or any other entity that plays a role in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the merchandise into the United States and has been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. CBP must provide the person with notification of the transmitted information.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee
posts.meta: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Blake Moore (R-UT)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) more power to get outside help when it suspects that imported goods infringe on trademarks or copyrights. Under current law, CBP can ask certain people, such as trademark or copyright owners, to help decide whether goods are illegal copies, and it can share specified label and packaging information so they can examine and test the goods. The bill widens both parts of that system.

First, it lets CBP ask for help from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported goods, not just the specified groups covered now. Second, it expands the information CBP can share to include information about and images of packing materials and containers, not only what appears on the goods and their labels.

The bill also lowers the threshold for asking for help. Right now CBP must suspect a violation. Under the bill, it may act if it has a reasonable suspicion that the goods violate certain trademark and copyright laws.

In addition, CBP may give a person nonpublic information about the imported goods that was generated by an online marketplace or similar platform, an express consignment operator, a freight forwarder, or any other entity involved in selling, importing, or moving the goods into the United States. That information must have been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. When CBP shares it, it must notify the person that the information was sent.

Disaster Communications Coordination and Preparedness Act
This bill directs the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to assess its procedures for disasters and emergencies affecting communications service and consider measures to improve coordination with officials and service providers during such events.
Specifically, the FCC must review and update, as appropriate, its procedures for notifying communications service providers about activations and deactivations of the Disaster Information Reporting System (DIRS). (DIRS is activated during severe weather and other events to enable providers to report outages and other service issues.)
Further, the FCC must provide plain-language resources for state, local, tribal, and territorial officials on federal communications and emergency coordination mechanisms available during disasters and emergencies. To the extent practicable, these materials must include information on DIRS, the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative (MDRI), and services that may be available to support public safety communications during such events, among other topics. (MDRI requires cell service providers to coordinate and share resources during emergencies.)
Finally, the FCC must consider enhancing its functions related to (1) informing state, local, tribal, and territorial officials of the status of communications services during disasters and emergencies; and (2) facilitating coordination between these officials and communications providers before, during, and after such events.

This bill asks the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to look at how it handles communications during disasters and emergencies, and to find ways to work better with local officials and phone and internet companies when those events happen.

First, the FCC must review and, where appropriate, update how it tells communications companies when the Disaster Information Reporting System (DIRS) is turned on or off. DIRS is switched on during severe weather and similar events so that providers can report outages and other service problems.

posts.title: NASA Transition Authorization Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Commerce, Science, and Transportation, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, S. Rept. 119-156
posts.summary:
NASA Transition Authorization Act of 2025
This bill reauthorizes through FY2025 the programs and activities of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). The bill also revises certain existing NASA programs and establishes new programs related to space exploration, research, and technology.
For example, the bill directs NASA to continue its efforts to support crewed lunar landings and Mars explorations, including through partnerships with the private sector (i.e., the Moon to Mars and Artemis programs).
The bill also requires NASA to maintain the capability for a continuous human presence in low-Earth orbit until and beyond the retirement of the International Space Station (ISS). NASA may solicit proposals for the development of a commercial space station in low-Earth orbit. When such a station is ready, NASA must initiate an orderly transition of operations from the ISS to the commercial station. NASA must also develop a de-orbit vehicle for the eventual retirement of the ISS. (Low-Earth orbit encompasses orbits at an altitude of 1,200 miles or less.)
In addition, NASA is authorized to develop an architecture for lunar communications and navigation, and must develop a strategy to implement a standardized lunar time to support operations and infrastructure on and around the moon.
NASA must also continue to conduct research relating to advanced air mobility, unmanned aircraft systems (i.e., drones), and hypersonic technologies.
Finally, the bill requires the Government Accountability Office to report on fire and emergency services at NASA launch and reentry facilities.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends NASA's existing programs and activities through fiscal year 2025, and it also changes some current programs and creates new ones focused on space exploration, research, and technology. It directs NASA to keep working toward crewed landings on the Moon and exploration of Mars, including through partnerships with private companies. These efforts fall under the Moon to Mars and Artemis programs.

The bill requires NASA to keep a continuous human presence in low-Earth orbit, meaning orbits at an altitude of 1,200 miles or less, until and beyond the retirement of the International Space Station (ISS). NASA may ask companies to propose a commercial space station in low-Earth orbit. Once that station is ready, NASA must begin an orderly move of operations from the ISS to it. NASA must also develop a de-orbit vehicle, a spacecraft that would bring the ISS down when it is eventually retired.

The bill also allows NASA to design a system for communications and navigation on the Moon. It requires NASA to develop a plan for a standard lunar time to support activities on and around the Moon.

In addition, NASA must keep researching advanced air mobility, unmanned aircraft systems (drones), and hypersonic technologies.

Finally, the Government Accountability Office must report on fire and emergency services at NASA's launch and reentry facilities.

posts.summary:
Spending Aviation Fees for Equipment, Guaranteeing Upgraded and Advanced Risk Detection and Safety Act of 2025 or the SAFEGUARDS Act of 2025
This bill allocates additional funding for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) for aviation security, including checked baggage explosives detection equipment and security checkpoint technology.
As background, TSA collects passenger civil aviation security service fees (often referred to as the 9/11 security fee or passenger security fee) on air carrier passengers originating at airports in the United States. In general, these fees are deposited into the Department of the Treasury general fund and applied towards debt reduction. A portion of these fees are allocated to TSA for aviation security.
The bill requires that the first $500 million collected in each fiscal year from passenger security fees be deposited into the Aviation Security Capital Fund. This is an increase from the currently required $250 million. This fund provides for the costs associated with acquiring and installing in-line baggage screening systems (i.e., systems that use a conveyor belt infrastructure to automatically screen, sort, and track baggage) to accommodate checked baggage explosives detection equipment and for certain other airport security improvements.
The bill also requires that the next $250 million collected in each fiscal year from passenger security fees be deposited into a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund for the costs associated with acquiring, deploying, and sustaining aviation security checkpoint and exit lane technology. TSA may use these funds retroactively for projects implemented on or after January 1, 2023.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate

aiSummaries.text:
The SAFEGUARDS Act of 2025 is meant to pay for better airport security equipment. It adds money for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to buy and maintain checked-baggage explosives detection machines and technology used at security checkpoints.

Right now, TSA collects a passenger security fee (often called the 9/11 security fee) from air travelers departing from U.S. airports. Most of that money goes into the Treasury's general fund and is used to reduce the federal debt, and only part of it is given to TSA for aviation security.

Under the bill, the first $500 million collected each fiscal year from these fees would go into an Aviation Security Capital Fund. That is up from the $250 million currently required. This fund pays for installing in-line baggage screening systems, which use conveyor belts to automatically screen, sort, and track checked bags, and for certain other airport security upgrades.

The next $250 million collected each year would go into a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund. This money would cover buying, setting up, and keeping in working order the technology used at security checkpoints and exit lanes. TSA could also use this fund for projects started on or after January 1, 2023.

posts.summary:
Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to increase the amounts payable for wartime disability compensation, additional compensation for dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation for surviving spouses and children. Specifically, the VA must increase the amounts by the same percentage as the cost-of-living increase in benefits for Social Security recipients that is effective on December 1, 2026. The act requires the VA to publish the amounts payable, as increased, in the Federal Register.
The VA is authorized to make a similar adjustment to the rates of disability compensation payable to persons who have not received compensation for service-connected disability or death.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House

aiSummaries.text:
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to raise several benefit payments for veterans and their families. The payments covered are wartime disability compensation, extra compensation for dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation for surviving spouses and children.

The increase is set by the same percentage as the cost-of-living increase for Social Security recipients that takes effect on December 1, 2026. In other words, the veterans' payments rise by that same percentage.

The VA must publish the new, higher payment amounts in the Federal Register, the official government publication where such notices appear.

The VA is also allowed, though not required, to make a similar adjustment to disability compensation rates for people who have not received compensation for a service-connected disability or death.

posts.title: America's National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark Act
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
America's National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark Act
This bill designates the America’s National Churchill Museum, including the Winston Churchill Memorial, located at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, as the America’s National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark. (Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill gave a speech titled The Sinews of Peace, also widely known as the Iron Curtain Speech, at the college in 1946.)
The bill permits the Department of the Interior to enter into cooperative agreements with public and private entities for the purposes of protecting historic resources at the landmark and providing educational and interpretive facilities for the public. Interior may provide technical and financial assistance to partner entities.
The bill also directs Interior to conduct a special resource study to evaluate the national significance of the landmark and to determine the suitability and feasibility of designating it as a unit of the National Park System. The study must consider alternatives to that designation for the preservation, protection, and interpretation of the landmark, and must include cost estimates associated with identified alternatives.

posts.title: Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Commerce, H. Rept. 119-872
posts.summary:
Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act
This bill expedites the process of reviewing certain uncontested permits and licenses for nuclear power plants (e.g., construction permits and operating licenses) by removing a requirement for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to hold a public hearing at the end of the process. The bill applies to the licenses and permits if a hearing has not been requested by a person whose interest may be affected. The bill also directs the NRC to use informal adjudicatory procedures if such a hearing is held.
Additionally, the bill directs the NRC to hold an adjudicatory hearing regarding the licensing of the construction and operation of a uranium enrichment facility only if the person whose interest may be affected by such construction and operation has requested the hearing.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. H. Griffith (R-VA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill speeds up how the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approves certain nuclear power plant permits and licenses, such as those for building a plant or running one. Normally the NRC holds a public hearing at the end of the review. Under this bill, that final hearing is no longer required for permits and licenses that no one has asked to contest, meaning no person whose interests could be affected has requested a hearing. When a hearing is held, the NRC must use informal procedures rather than formal ones.

The bill also changes the rules for uranium enrichment facilities, which are plants that process uranium. For these, the NRC holds an adjudicatory hearing on the building and operation of the facility only if a person whose interests may be affected by it has asked for one.

posts.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 and revises programs that support research and development of drugs and other therapies to address amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (also known as ALS or Lou Gehrig's disease) and other neurodegenerative diseases.
The bill reauthorizes
grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for scientific research on investigational drugs to prevent or treat ALS for individuals not otherwise eligible for clinical trials,
grants from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for research and development of therapies to prevent and treat ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases, and
a Public-Private Partnership including the FDA and NIH that supports development and regulatory review of treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
Also, the NIH, in considering renewal of its grants, must assess available information on the safety and efficacy of the investigational drugs. It must also require grantees to promptly report serious and unexpected adverse events associated with their investigational drugs.
Additionally, the FDA must publish a plan describing actions it will take over a five-year period to foster development of safe and effective drugs, and facilitate access to investigational drugs, that treat ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases. The FDA must also publish a report describing the actions it has taken under the plan.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Mike Quigley (D-IL)
posts.whatsNext: Takes effect (on enactment unless the text sets other dates)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends several federal programs through fiscal year 2031 that fund research and development of drugs and other treatments for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease) and other brain-related diseases that get worse over time.

Three programs are renewed. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) can keep giving grants for research on experimental drugs to prevent or treat ALS for people who can't otherwise join clinical trials. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) can keep giving grants to develop therapies for ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases. A public-private partnership involving the FDA and NIH can also keep supporting the development and regulatory review of treatments for these diseases.

The bill adds some safety requirements. When the NIH decides whether to renew one of these grants, it must review the available information on how safe and effective the experimental drug is. It must also require grant recipients to report serious and unexpected side effects promptly.

The FDA must publish a five-year plan describing what it will do to encourage the development of safe and effective drugs for ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases, and to make experimental drugs easier to access. Afterward, it must publish a report on the actions it has taken under that plan.
